notes.definition: In chemistry, a pure substance is a single element or a single compound that is not mixed with any other substance. Pure elements and compounds melt and boil at specific, fixed temperatures, so melting point and boiling point data can be used to tell a pure substance from a mixture.
explanation: The word 'pure' means something different in chemistry from its everyday meaning. In everyday language, a pure substance is one that has had nothing added to it, so it is unadulterated and in its natural state. 'Pure' orange juice or 'pure' milk are examples, but both are mixtures of many different compounds dissolved or suspended in water. A chemist would not call them pure, because they contain more than one substance.

In chemistry, a pure substance contains only one element or only one compound. Pure oxygen gas contains only O₂ molecules. Pure water contains only H₂O molecules. Sodium chloride is a compound made from two elements chemically combined, but a sample of pure sodium chloride contains only NaCl, so it is still a pure substance. A mixture contains two or more elements or compounds that are not chemically combined, such as air, sea water or an alloy.

Every pure element or compound has a specific melting point and a specific boiling point at a given pressure. For example, pure water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at normal atmospheric pressure. When a pure solid is heated, its temperature stays constant while it melts, because the energy supplied is used to overcome the forces between particles rather than to raise the temperature. This gives a sharp melting point.

A mixture does not have a single sharp melting point. It usually melts gradually over a range of temperatures, and that range is usually lower than the melting point of the main pure substance. Impurities also tend to raise the boiling point and make a liquid boil over a range of temperatures. Salt water, for example, boils above 100 °C. Ice with salt on it melts below 0 °C, which is why salt is spread on icy roads.

Chemists use these facts to test purity. A sample's melting point can be measured and compared with the data book value for the pure substance. If the sample melts sharply at exactly the expected temperature, it is likely to be pure. If it melts over a range of temperatures, or below the expected value, it is impure. This is important in making medicines, where the drug must be pure and contain no harmful by-products.
keyFacts: A pure substance (chemistry meaning) is a single element or a single compound not mixed with anything else.
In everyday language, 'pure' means nothing has been added, or the substance is in its natural state (for example 'pure milk').
Pure substances melt and boil at specific, fixed temperatures.
Mixtures (impure substances) melt and boil over a range of temperatures.
Impurities usually lower the melting point and raise the boiling point.
Pure water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at atmospheric pressure.
Comparing a measured melting point with data book values tells you whether a sample is pure.
A compound can be pure: pure sodium chloride contains only NaCl.

keyTerms.definition: In chemistry, a single element or compound that is not mixed with any other substance.
Two or more elements or compounds that are not chemically combined together.
The specific temperature at which a pure solid turns into a liquid.
The specific temperature at which a pure liquid boils and turns into a gas throughout the liquid.
An unwanted substance mixed with the substance of interest; it changes the melting and boiling points.
A substance made of two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.

workedExamples.title: Using melting point data
workedExamples.question: Pure aspirin melts at 136 °C. Sample A melts at 136 °C. Sample B melts between 128 °C and 133 °C. Which sample is pure? Explain.
steps: A pure substance melts at a specific temperature that matches the data book value.
Sample A melts sharply at 136 °C, exactly the value for pure aspirin.
Sample B melts over a range (128 to 133 °C), and the range is below 136 °C. Both features show impurities.
workedExamples.answer: Sample A is pure; sample B is impure because it melts over a range of temperatures below the melting point of pure aspirin.

workedExamples.title: Interpreting a heating curve
workedExamples.question: A student heats two solids and records temperature against time. Solid X has a flat section at 80 °C. Solid Y has no flat section; its temperature rises slowly from 70 °C to 77 °C while it melts. Which solid is a mixture?
steps: A flat section on a heating curve shows a fixed melting point: temperature stays constant while the solid melts.
Solid X therefore has a fixed melting point of 80 °C, so it is pure.
Solid Y melts over a range of temperatures, 70 to 77 °C, so it contains more than one substance.

workedExamples.title: Chemical versus everyday meaning
workedExamples.question: A carton is labelled '100% pure apple juice'. Explain why a chemist would not describe the juice as pure.
steps: In everyday language, 'pure' means nothing has been added to the juice.
In chemistry, a pure substance contains only one element or one compound.
Apple juice contains water, sugars, acids, vitamins and other compounds, so it is a mixture.
workedExamples.answer: The juice is a mixture of many compounds, so it is not pure in the chemical sense, even though nothing has been added.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a compound cannot be pure because it contains more than one element.
misconceptions.right: In fact a pure compound, such as pure water or pure sodium chloride, contains only one substance, so it is pure. The elements in it are chemically combined, not mixed.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think products labelled 'pure', such as 'pure orange juice', are pure substances.
misconceptions.right: In fact the everyday meaning is 'nothing added'. Orange juice is a mixture of water, sugars, acids and many other compounds.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think impurities raise the melting point.
misconceptions.right: In fact impurities usually lower the melting point and make the substance melt over a range of temperatures; they usually raise the boiling point.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think 'clear and colourless' means a liquid is pure.
misconceptions.right: In fact a solution such as salt water can look clear and colourless. Only melting or boiling point data (or other analysis) can show purity.

realWorld: Pharmaceutical companies measure the melting points of drugs to check they are pure before they are made into tablets.
Salt is spread on icy roads because the dissolved salt lowers the melting point of ice below 0 °C.
Food labels use 'pure' in the everyday sense (nothing added), which is why honey or juice labelled 'pure' is still a mixture.
examTips: When asked to define a pure substance, write 'a single element or a single compound, not mixed with any other substance'. Saying 'nothing added' is the everyday meaning and gains no marks.
When using data to judge purity, compare with the known value AND comment on whether it melts at a fixed point or over a range.
On heating or cooling curves, a flat section means a fixed melting or boiling point (pure); a sloping section during the change of state means a mixture.
Say impurities 'lower' the melting point and 'raise' the boiling point; do not just say they 'change' it.
summary: Chemically pure: one element or one compound only.
Pure substances have fixed, sharp melting and boiling points.
Mixtures melt and boil over a range of temperatures.
Impurities lower melting points and raise boiling points.
Compare measured melting points with data book values to test purity.

flashcards.front: What is a pure substance in chemistry?
flashcards.back: A single element or a single compound, not mixed with any other substance.

flashcards.front: What does 'pure' mean in everyday language?
flashcards.back: A substance that has had nothing added to it and is in its natural state, for example 'pure milk'.

flashcards.front: How do impurities affect melting point?
flashcards.back: They usually lower it and make it a range.

flashcards.front: How do impurities affect boiling point?
Melting and boiling points of pure water?
Is pure sodium chloride a pure substance?
flashcards.back: Yes: it contains only one compound, NaCl.
No: it is a mixture of gases such as nitrogen, oxygen, argon and carbon dioxide.

flashcards.front: What does a flat section on a heating curve show?
flashcards.back: A fixed melting (or boiling) point, so the substance is pure.

flashcards.front: How can you test whether a solid is pure?
flashcards.back: Measure its melting point and compare it with the data book value for the pure substance.

flashcards.front: Why is salt spread on icy roads?
flashcards.back: Salt is an impurity that lowers the melting point of ice, so it melts below 0 °C.

questions.question: Which of these is a pure substance in the chemical sense?
markScheme: 1 mark: Distilled water
questions.explanation: Distilled water contains only H₂O molecules. Sea water and orange juice contain many dissolved substances, and air is a mixture of gases.

questions.question: What is the meaning of 'pure substance' in chemistry?
options: A substance with nothing added to it
A substance that is safe to eat or drink
A single element or compound not mixed with any other substance
markScheme: 1 mark: A single element or compound not mixed with any other substance
questions.explanation: The chemical meaning is one element or one compound only. 'Nothing added' and 'natural' are everyday meanings.

questions.question: How does a pure solid behave when it is heated to its melting point?
options: It melts at a specific temperature
It melts over a wide range of temperatures
Its temperature rises quickly while it melts
markScheme: 1 mark: It melts at a specific temperature
questions.explanation: Pure substances have fixed melting points. Mixtures melt over a range. While melting, the temperature stays constant.

questions.question: A label says 'pure honey'. What does 'pure' mean on this label?
options: Nothing has been added to the honey
Honey has a fixed boiling point
markScheme: 1 mark: Nothing has been added to the honey
questions.explanation: On food labels 'pure' is the everyday meaning: nothing added. Honey is a mixture of sugars, water and other compounds.

questions.question: Pure ethanoic acid melts at 17 °C. Which result shows a sample is impure?
options: Melts sharply at 17 °C and boils at 118 °C
markScheme: 1 mark: Melts between 12 °C and 15 °C
questions.explanation: An impure sample melts over a range of temperatures, usually lower than the pure value. 12 to 15 °C is a range below 17 °C.

questions.question: Which of these is a pure compound?
options: Brass (an alloy of copper and zinc)
Sodium chloride crystals with nothing else present
markScheme: 1 mark: Sodium chloride crystals with nothing else present
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride is a compound and on its own it is pure. Oxygen is a pure element, not a compound. Brass and salt solution are mixtures.

questions.question: What usually happens to the boiling point of water when salt is dissolved in it?
options: The water can no longer boil
markScheme: 1 mark: It goes up
questions.explanation: Impurities raise the boiling point, so salt water boils above 100 °C. They lower the melting point.

questions.question:
A student heated a solid and recorded its temperature every minute.
Figure 1 shows the student's heating curve.
Which feature shows that the solid is pure?
options: The curve starts at room temperature
There is a horizontal section at one temperature while it melts
The curve has a gentle slope while the solid melts
markScheme: 1 mark: There is a horizontal section at one temperature while it melts
questions.explanation: A horizontal section means the temperature stays constant during melting, which is a fixed melting point. A slope during melting indicates a mixture.

questions.question: Pure substance P melts at 122 °C. A sample of P is contaminated with a small amount of Q. Which melting point is the most likely for the contaminated sample?
markScheme: 1 mark: 118 to 121 °C
questions.explanation: Impurities lower the melting point and make it melt over a range, so a range just below 122 °C is expected. A range above it would not be typical.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a pure substance in chemistry?
markScheme: 1 mark: Milk
questions.explanation: Milk is a mixture of water, fats, proteins and sugars. The others are single elements or a single compound.

questions.question: Give the chemical definition of a pure substance.
acceptedAnswers: not mixed with any other substance
markScheme: 1 mark: a single element or a single compound, not mixed with any other substance
questions.explanation: This is the definition in the AQA specification. Answers like 'nothing added' are the everyday meaning and do not score.

questions.question: State the melting point and boiling point of pure water at atmospheric pressure.
markScheme: 1 mark: melting point 0 °C
1 mark: boiling point 100 °C
questions.explanation: These are fixed values for pure water. Impure water, such as sea water, has a lower melting point and a higher boiling point.

questions.question: Explain why 'pure apple juice' is not a pure substance in chemistry.
markScheme: 1 mark: a pure substance contains only one element or compound
1 mark: apple juice contains several substances (for example water and sugars), so it is a mixture
questions.explanation: Food manufacturers use 'pure' to mean nothing added, but the juice still contains many different compounds.

questions.question: Describe how you could use a melting point measurement to find out if a sample of a solid is pure.
acceptedAnswers: pure melts at a fixed temperature
markScheme: 1 mark: measure the melting point (temperature at which it melts) and compare it with the known value for the pure substance
1 mark: pure if it melts sharply at that value; impure if it melts over a range or below the known value
questions.explanation: Pure substances have a specific melting point. Impurities lower the melting point and spread it over a range.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows melting point data for a pure substance and for a sample of the same substance.
Give two pieces of evidence from Table 1 that the sample is impure.
markScheme: 1 mark: it melts over a range of temperatures (not a single temperature)
1 mark: it melts below the melting point of the pure substance
questions.explanation: Both features are typical of a mixture: impurities lower the melting point and make it melt over a range.

questions.question: Salt is spread on roads in winter. Suggest why this stops ice forming at 0 °C.
markScheme: 1 mark: the salt (an impurity) lowers the melting/freezing point of water, so salty water freezes below 0 °C
questions.explanation: Impurities lower the melting point, so ice in contact with salt melts even below 0 °C.

questions.question: A pure solid is heated steadily. Explain why its temperature stays constant while it is melting, and why a mixture behaves differently.
acceptedAnswers: energy used to overcome forces between particles
markScheme: 1 mark: energy supplied is used to overcome the forces (attractions) between the particles
1 mark: so the temperature does not rise until all the solid has melted, giving a fixed melting point
1 mark: a mixture contains different substances (with different particles and forces), so it melts gradually over a range of temperatures
questions.explanation: During a change of state, energy goes into breaking forces between particles. In a mixture the particles are not all the same, so melting is spread over a range.

questions.question: Classify each of these as a pure substance or a mixture: (a) steel, (b) iron, (c) carbon dioxide, (d) crude oil.
markScheme: 2 marks: all four correct (steel mixture, iron pure, carbon dioxide pure, crude oil mixture)
1 mark: two or three correct
questions.explanation: Steel is an alloy (mixture) of iron with carbon and other elements. Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons. Iron is an element and carbon dioxide is a compound.

questions.question:
Two white powders, X and Y, look identical.
Both are thought to be the same compound, which melts at 160 °C.
Table 1 shows the melting points of X and Y.
A student says Y is a different compound.
Evaluate the student's conclusion.
acceptedAnswers: could be the same compound but impure
melts over a range so it is a mixture
markScheme: 1 mark: Y melts over a range and below 160 °C, so it is impure (a mixture)
1 mark: it may be the same compound containing impurities, so the conclusion is not justified without further tests (for example chromatography)
questions.explanation: Melting over a range below the expected value shows impurities, not necessarily a different compound. The main component could still be the expected compound.

questions.question: Name the type of substance that melts over a range of temperatures.
markScheme: 1 mark: a mixture / impure substance
questions.explanation: Only pure substances have sharp, fixed melting points.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows data for a colourless liquid at atmospheric pressure.
What can you conclude about the liquid?
options: It is very likely to be pure water
It is a mixture of water and ethanol
markScheme: 1 mark: It is very likely to be pure water
questions.explanation: These are the fixed points of pure water. Mixtures would boil above 100 °C or freeze below 0 °C. Water is a compound, not an element.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the melting points of four samples, A, B, C and D, of a drug.
The pure drug melts at 135 °C.
Which sample is most likely to contain the largest amount of impurity?
markScheme: 1 mark: C
questions.explanation: More impurity generally gives a lower melting point and a wider range. C has the widest range and lowest temperature. A is pure.

questions.question: Which statement about the temperature of a pure liquid while it is boiling is correct?
options: It stays constant at the boiling point
It falls because energy is lost
markScheme: 1 mark: It stays constant at the boiling point
questions.explanation: While a pure liquid boils, energy is used to overcome forces between particles, so temperature stays constant at the boiling point.

questions.question:
A student cooled some molten wax and recorded its temperature.
Figure 1 shows the student's results.
Suggest what Figure 1 tells you about the wax.
Explain your answer.
markScheme: 1 mark: the wax is a mixture (not pure)
1 mark: a pure substance would show a flat section at its fixed freezing/melting point; the wax solidifies over a range of temperatures
questions.explanation: Paraffin wax is a mixture of hydrocarbons, so it has no sharp freezing point.

questions.question: Compare the meaning of the word 'pure' in everyday language and in chemistry. Use examples in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: everyday 'pure' means nothing added or in its natural state
Example: pure milk, pure orange juice, pure honey
These are mixtures of many substances (water, fats, sugars, proteins)
Chemistry: a pure substance is a single element or a single compound not mixed with anything else
Examples: pure water (only H₂O), oxygen, sodium chloride
Pure substances have fixed melting and boiling points; everyday 'pure' products melt or boil over a range
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear comparison of both meanings with correct examples of each
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one meaning given correctly, or both given with no examples
questions.explanation: A good answer states both meanings, gives an example of each, and explains that 'pure' food products are mixtures in the chemical sense.

questions.question: A company makes paracetamol. Pure paracetamol melts at 169 °C. Describe how the company could use melting and boiling point data to check the purity of a batch, and explain how the results would show whether the batch is pure or impure.
markScheme: Indicative content: take a small dry sample of the batch
Heat it slowly (for example in a melting point apparatus or water/oil bath) with a thermometer
Record the temperature at which melting starts and finishes
Compare with the data value for pure paracetamol (169 °C)
Pure: melts sharply at a single temperature equal to 169 °C
Impure: melts over a range of temperatures
Impure: melting begins below 169 °C; more impurity gives lower and wider ranges
Explanation: pure substances have fixed melting points because all particles are the same; mixtures do not
Boiling point could also be checked: impurities raise the boiling point
Repeat to check results are repeatable
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): clear, logical method and full explanation of how pure and impure results differ, with reasons
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): method described and results interpreted with some explanation
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example 'measure the melting point'
questions.explanation: Top answers link the method to the scientific idea that only pure substances have fixed melting points, and describe both lower and wider melting ranges for impure batches.

questions.question: Which of these is a mixture?
markScheme: 1 mark: Air
questions.explanation: Air contains several gases mixed together. Gold and oxygen are elements, and water is a compound.
